title: Micro SaaS: how to turn what you already know how to do into recurring revenue
excerpt: Every month you solve the same problem for the same kind of client. A micro SaaS turns that routine into a product that bills on its own, month after month.
content:
There's a spreadsheet, a playbook, or a method inside your company that solves one specific problem really well. Every month you repeat that process for the same kind of client, charging by the hour, by the project, or by the consultation. Now answer honestly: why isn't this a product yet?

The question stings because the answer is usually "I never stopped to think about it". And while nobody thinks about it, the knowledge stays locked in one person's head, earning money only during the hours that person is available. A micro SaaS is exactly the way out of that limit.

What a micro SaaS is

A micro SaaS is a small piece of software, sold by subscription, that solves a single problem really well for a very specific audience. It doesn't try to be a complete management system, it doesn't have fifty modules, and it doesn't need a big team to exist. It usually grows out of a pain the owner deals with in their own operation, and it's run by one person or a few.

The word micro isn't about quality or revenue. It's about scope. Small scope, big focus.

Five signs there's a micro SaaS inside your business

  1. You repeat the same manual work for different clients. Same spreadsheet, same calculation, same report, with only the numbers changing.
  2. Clients ask for "that file of yours". When something you created has become a reference, it already has the value of a product.
  3. Big systems ignore your niche. Generic tools serve everyone more or less, and nobody well.
  4. You charge by the hour and your calendar is the ceiling. Revenue that only grows with more hours has its limit written all over it.
  5. Someone has already asked if they could sign up for it monthly. That's the clearest sign of all, and also the most wasted.

Why recurring revenue changes the game

Selling projects means starting from zero every month. You close, deliver, celebrate, and on the first day of the next month the counter goes back to zero. Subscriptions work the other way around: the January client keeps paying in February, and the February client adds on top. Growth stops being a series of spikes and becomes a staircase.

There's a side effect people rarely talk about. With predictable revenue, you stop taking on bad projects just to make the month work. Recurring revenue buys you the freedom to choose, and that's often worth more than the subscription itself.

What changes in practice

  • Your knowledge starts working without you having to be there.
  • Price stops being negotiated by the hour and starts being negotiated by results.
  • Each new client costs less to serve than the last one.
  • The product becomes an asset, with its own value, that could even be sold one day.
  • You stop being an occasional supplier and become part of the client's routine.

What it costs to keep charging by the hour

Do the math. Take the number of clients you serve today with the same repeated process and multiply it by a modest monthly subscription, somewhere between R$ 100 and R$ 300. Multiply that by twelve months. Now compare it with what that same group paid for one-off services last year. In most cases the recurring amount is lower per client, higher in total, and it comes in without eating up your calendar. The gap between those two numbers is the price the hourly model is charging you.

When a micro SaaS doesn't make sense

If the problem you solve changes completely with each client, if delivery depends on human judgment at every step, or if you don't have a stable process down on paper yet, now isn't the time. Software automates processes, not improvisation. Before it becomes a product, the method has to exist and work the same way a few dozen times. If that method still lives in a spreadsheet today, the first step is usually a custom system for your own operation, and the product comes later.

It's also worth stating the obvious: a micro SaaS isn't quick money. It's a product, and a product takes support, continuous improvement, and patience in the first months of operation.

How a project like this works

  1. Narrowing down. We pick a single problem and a single audience. Nothing more than that in the first version.
  2. Mapping the operation. We map your current process, from the first click to the delivered result.
  3. A lean first version. Sign-up, recurring billing, and the core feature working. No frills.
  4. First subscribers. It starts with people who are already your clients, because they trust you and will point out what's missing.
  5. Evolving with data. What subscribers use becomes the priority. What nobody opens gets removed.

A service sells your time. A product sells your method. If you already have a method and keep selling time, you're funding your own ceiling.

Where to start

Open your calendar for the last ninety days and look for the task that repeated the most. That's candidate number one. Write in one sentence what problem it solves and for whom, and you already have a draft of the product.
